chapter_theme: Eleven fragments of lost Paripadal songs, kept by later writers: a prayer to the Vaigai, the flood likened to the Pandya's cavalry, a dancer or bride and her ornaments, and a run of city praises in which Koodal outweighs the world, is laid out as Mayon's lotus, outlasts the king's hill, river and word, outranks heaven by honouring giver and receiver, and bewilders its own people with pleasures.

thirattu:3.reading: With the righteous there to guard the rare scripture, the speaker prays that the close bond between us, which no enemy could wish to break, be joined to us again in the next round as well, and that the cool-flowing Vaigai of excellent course be ours.

thinai_evidence.note: a closing prayer addressed through the river, the vaazhthu of paadaan

thirattu:3.nuance: மறுமுறை may mean the next birth or simply the next turn of the festival, when the bathers hope to come to the river again; the lost line 2 kept whatever joined the guardians of the scripture to the prayer, so the bond (நங் கேண்மை) may be the lovers' or the worshippers' with the river.

thirattu:4.reading: The Vaigai spread out like the ranks of horses of the Pandya, lord of the southern mountain, who is versed in the threefold Tamil.

thinai_evidence.note: the river is praised through the king's own cavalry

comparisons.tenor: the Vaigai's flood spreading over its bed

thirattu:4.nuance: The king is named not by conquest but by learning (தெரிமாண் தமிழ் மும்மை, the threefold Tamil of verse, song and drama), and the flood borrows its force from his horses, so river, king and Tamil are praised in one breath.

thirattu:5.reading: Addressing a lovely woman whose shoulders keep time with the clay-smeared drum and fall in unison with it without her seeming to heed, the speaker asks whether the hearts of those who watch her can stay with them.
thirattu:5.nuance: The syntax of lines 1 and 2 is open: கொண்ட தோள் may be her shoulders moving with the drum in a dance, or a man's drum-like shoulders into whose embrace she falls without a thought; on either reading the closing question turns her beauty into the onlookers' loss of heart, the love-at-sight that the fragment leaves without a named lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the first union, never known before, is the kalavu meeting of kurinji

thirattu:6.reading: At a first union she had never known before, the girl with thick tresses wore with joy her natural beauty and her strong jewels, and with them modesty, called her ancient ornament; the rest of the line is lost.
thirattu:6.nuance: Three ornaments are ranked: the beauty she was born with (இயல் அணி), the jewels she put on (வன் பணி), and modesty, which is called older than both (தொல்லை அணி), so the shame that might seem to hold her back at the first union is counted as her oldest adornment.

thirattu:7.reading: When poets set the world in one pan and the city in the other and weighed them with the balance of their learning, the whole world drooped while the Pandya's four-towered Koodal stayed unfaded.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the Pandya's city by a weighing that the poets make

comparisons.tenor: the poets' judgment as a balance beam

comparisons.vehicle: உலகம் ஒரு நிறையாத் தான் ஓர் நிறையா
comparisons.tenor: the world and the city as the two weights set against each other

thirattu:7.nuance: வாட does double work: in a balance the pan that goes down is the heavier, but வாடு is also to wither, so the world 'sinks' and 'fades' at once while Koodal, the one that does not fade (வாடாத), is praised for a permanence the scale cannot measure; the judges are poets, not kings.

thirattu:8.reading: Our great town is like the lotus that blossomed from Mayon's navel: its streets are the petals, the lord's palace the pericarp, its Tamil households the pollen and those who live on gifts the bees that eat it; it wakes from its safe sweet sleep only to the voices reciting the four Vedas born from the tongue of Brahma born in that flower, and not, like Vanji and Kozhi, to the cock's crow.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the city laid out as one flower

comparisons.tenor: the lord's palace at the centre
the way the town wakes (by contrast)

thirattu:8.nuance: The flower is a map of a society: palace at the centre, households as the pollen that is the flower's wealth, and gift-seekers as the bees that feed on the households, not on the palace. The last lines pun on கோழி, the Chola city Uraiyur and the cock (line 11): the rival capitals wake to a bird, Madurai to the Veda, so the praise ranks the three capitals by the sound each wakes to.

thirattu:9.reading: Can Madurai ever decline, rather than stand firm and blossom in fame throughout the Tamil land fenced by cool Tamil, as long as the hill of the king with the bannered chariot endures?

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing on the city's lasting fame

comparisons.tenor: Tamil as the boundary that encloses the Tamil land

thirattu:9.nuance: The land is fenced not by mountains or sea but by its language (தண் தமிழ் வேலி). This is the first of three fragments built on one frame (thirattu 9, 10, 11): each ends 'as long as the king's ... exists', and the measure moves from the hill to the river to his word. Whose hill is meant (the Pandya's, or the god's Parankundram) the fragment does not settle.

thirattu:10.reading: Like the tilaka drawn on the brow of the lady of fortune, matching her beauty, Madurai lights the world and blossoms in fame; can it ever prove false as long as the Vaigai of the king of the adorned chariot flows?

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing on the city's lasting fame

comparisons.tenor: Madurai on the face of the world

thirattu:10.nuance: The world is the goddess's face and Madurai the mark at its centre: the simile makes the city the one point that gives the whole its auspiciousness, and பொய்யாதல் ('turning false') treats fame as a promise the city keeps.

thirattu:11.reading: Like the heavy makara earring on the ear of Karthigai, Madurai shines in excellence and blossoms in prosperity; can any loss come to it as long as the word of the king of the bannered chariot stands?

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing on the city's lasting prosperity

thirattu:11.nuance: கோத்தை is a rare word; its place in the frame, where the sister fragments have குன்றுதல் (decline) and பொய்யாதல் (proving false), fixes it as loss or defect. Karthigai is the asterism pictured as a woman, so the city is a jewel in the sky's ear. The third measure is வார்த்தை, the king's word or renown, so the city's endurance ends tied to speech rather than to hill or river.

thirattu:12.reading: High-towered Koodal and the red Vel's Parankundram, which honour those who give and rejoice to see those who receive: those who live there are the ones rightly called living, and who among the rest would go to the world of the gods?

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the city and the god's hill above heaven

thirattu:12.nuance: The city is praised for rejoicing at the sight of receivers (ஏற்பாரைப் பார்த்து உவக்கும்), not only at givers: asking is part of the honoured life, not its shame. Line 4 is compressed; it may ask who would go to the gods' world, or who among those not living there is going to it, but either way heaven is ranked below life in Koodal.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers' dilemma is offered as the nature of the city, a praise of Koodal

thirattu:13.reading: Is it sweeter to bathe in the Vaigai's rising flood, or to enjoy the hill of the king of the red spear, and how shall we spend it with women whose eyes are like the sharp spear's point as our companions? To be lost every day in such doubt about which way to go is the nature of tall-towered Koodal of Nediyon.
thirattu:13.nuance: The praise is put as a complaint: the city has so many pleasures (river, sacred hill, women) that its people lose their way among them daily (வழி மயக்குற்று மருடல்). The love matter is the city's, not a lover's: no one is parted, and the choice of pleasures is itself the proof of Koodal's plenty. நெடியான் may be Thirumal or the Pandya.

links.note: Kural 118 likens the worthy man's impartiality to a balance that levels itself before it weighs; thirattu 7 has poets weigh the world against Koodal with the balance of their learning (புலக் கோலால் தூக்க).
links.teaches: Read beside the Kural's just balance, the fragment's praise borrows the authority of an impartial weighing, so the poets present their verdict on Koodal as fairness, the ornament of the worthy, rather than as a court singer's flattery.

links.note: Kalittokai 35 line 2 likens humming bees in the boughs to the enjoyment of those who live on a diligent man's wealth; thirattu 8 likens those who live on gifts (பரிசில் வாழ்நர்) to bees eating pollen.
links.teaches: The bee and the dependent were interchangeable figures that ran in both directions, a season described through patronage in Kalittokai and a society through a flower in the Paripadal, and only the Paripadal says whom the dependents feed on: the households, not the palace.

links.note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame; thirattu 9 says Madurai's fame will stand and blossom as long as the king's hill exists (குன்றம் உண்டாகும் அளவு).
links.teaches: The Kural makes fame the one thing that does not perish, while the Paripadal blessing gives even the city's fame a term measured by a hill, so the poets' praise of undying renown was bounded by the oldest lasting things of the land.

links.note: Thirattu 9, 10 and 11 share one frame ('can Madurai decline ... as long as the king's ... exists'); 9 measures it by his hill, 10 by his Vaigai, 11 by his word (வார்த்தை).
links.teaches: Taken as a set, the fragments move the city's guarantee from a hill and a river to the king's word, so the last stanza rests Madurai's permanence on speech and renown, the poet's own stock, rather than on the land.

links.note: Purananuru 38 says bards think of Killivalavan's land even in the gods' golden grove, because there no one with means gives and no one in want asks (உடையோர் ஈதலும் இல்லோர் இரத்தலும்); thirattu 12 says Koodal honours givers and rejoices at receivers, so who would go to the gods' world (புத்தேள் உலகு)?
links.teaches: Purananuru 38 supplies the reason the fragment leaves unsaid, that heaven is poorer for lacking the exchange of giving and asking, so the Paripadal's preference for Koodal over heaven rests on an older argument first made for a king's land and here transferred to a city and its god's hill.

links.note: Kural 222 says taking is bad even if called the good path to heaven, and giving good even if there were no higher world; thirattu 12 praises a city that rejoices to see receivers (ஏற்பாரைப் பார்த்து உவக்கும்) and ranks its life above heaven. On the reading that ஏற்பார் are those who take gifts, the fragment honours the very taking the Kural calls bad.
links.teaches: Both cut the value of giving loose from heaven, but the Kural does it by condemning the receiver while the Paripadal makes the receiver's presence a joy of the city, so the two hold opposite views of whether asking belongs to the good life.

links.note: Kural 1014 asks whether shame (நாணுடைமை) is not an ornament of the worthy; thirattu 6 calls modesty the girl's ancient ornament (நாண் எனும் தொல்லை அணி) at her first union.
links.teaches: The same figure of shame as an ornament serves the Kural for the moral restraint of the worthy and the Paripadal for a bride's reserve at first union, which shows that naanam named both and that the poets ranked the bride's reserve above her jewels as the Kural ranks restraint above pride.

links.note: Kalittokai 35 counts Koodal's seasonal pleasures (bees on the Vaigai's sandbank, the festival, the townsmen savouring poets' new words) as the times the absent man promised to return; thirattu 13 lists the Vaigai flood, the god's hill and spear-eyed women as pleasures among which Koodal's people lose their way daily.
links.teaches: The same catalogue of Koodal's pleasures marks the hour of a promised return in the Kalittokai and causes daily indecision in the Paripadal, so the city's festive plenty was a stock that akam used to sharpen absence and city praise used to show abundance.

source_issues: Paripadal thirattu 3 line 2 is lost (a line of dots); the link between the guardians of the scripture in line 1 and the prayer of lines 3 to 5 is gone.
Paripadal thirattu 6 line 3 has a gap before ...னந்து; the end of the sentence is lost.
Paripadal thirattu 4 line 1 and thirattu 5 line 2: TSCII leftovers repaired (flags).
Paripadal thirattu 8 line 11 (கோழியின் எழாது, எம் பேர் ஊர் துயிலே) is not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flag).
Paripadal thirattu 3 to 13 are fragments with no colophon thinai or thurai; the subject field (வையை, மதுரை) is given for only three of them, though thirattu 8 to 13 are also about Madurai.
